Story Time: When I was a third year medical student on my general surgery rotation, I met many individuals who stuck things where they shouldn't, and needed assistance. Anyone familiar with medical school knows that being the lowest raking learner on a team dedicated to colo-rectal health will put that learner in situations he/she never imagined.

After a long day of disimpacting old person colons, and digitally rectally examining enough rectums that my index finger was subjectively warmer than the rest of my hand (you can't wash the shame away, no matter how hard you scrub), I got paged by my senior at shortly after nine at night, to go and see a forty something year old man for bleeding, and foreign body in rectum (FBR). I hadn't eaten and since that morning, and needless to say was less than enthusiastic for my new assignment. I left whatever garbage paperwork I was doing and dutifully headed down to the ER.

I found the referring physician and medical student, a classmate of mine, to get the story before I went to see the patient. Long story short... a forty something male had "fallen" on a soy sauce bottle, and it broke inside of his rectum. As there was a small amount of blood from his anus, they didn't feel comfortable attempting to remove it without the opinion of my supervisor/team. As they were telling me the story, they brought up the abdominal x ray. It showed what I later found out while watching surgery was a 20 oz Kikkoman soy sauce bottle. It was wedged in his rectum, and the neck of the bottle was broken off in the sigmoid colon, as best as the ER doctor could determine from x-rays.

John, not his real name, was one of 8 people I saw in 30 days, who mysteriously "fell" on something, that ended up in his/her rectum. John was not a small man. He was a 6'5", solidly built man, whom I found out later was an enforcer for a local motorcycle enthusiasts' organization. I will not mention which one, out of fear for my own safety, and consideration for John (mostly fear for my own safety). I should note that the vast majority of bikers, though individuals that I would not wish to meet in a dark alley when I owe them money, are quite polite to health professionals. The truly dangerous ones always are. The loud skinny kid, running his mouth about how tough he is, will do something stupid, and might even assault someone in the ER, but is not capable of as much damage as a quiet, polite man-mountain when he is disturbed. I digress...

John and I didn't talk about how the bottle ended up broken in his rectum until the day after his surgery. Things had gone as well as could be expected when someone breaks a glass bottle (thankfully not containing soy sauce at the time it happened). John had a mid-line lower abdominal scar, and thankfully avoided having to have a colostomy. He was really grateful, but terrified that his fellow motorcycle enthusiasts would find out where he was and why he was there.

It was about ten in the morning, and I was checking on a different patient when John saw me in the hallway, and called me to his room. He wanted to make sure that we believed him that he was recycling when he slipped and the bottle popped into his rectum and broke. I stopped him from explaining/lying to me further. I was too tired (I had two hours of broken sleep that night), and had better things to do than be lied to, so I stopped him:

"John... None of us care whether or not you were recycling, or what exactly you were doing when this happened. It's non of our business, and we won't tell anyone. Most people don't recycle glass bottles by looping dental floss over the neck of the bottle. However you chose to reduce, reuse, or recycle is your business. If you are going to continue to "recycle", I need you to buy appropriate items to "recycle" from one of the many local stores that sells them, or even an online store, as you and I both know that dental floss did not lead to safe recycling yesterday."

After the words came out of my mouth, I was suddenly aware that I was alone with John, and no one was around to help me if he chose to break my neck. After what felt like the longest pause ever, John tilted his head, stroked his manly beard, and then nodded in agreement. In his deep voice he said, "Good to know". I asked him if he had any other questions, and he wanted to know about which online store I would recommend. Given that I had done my "research", with assistance from some of the general surgery floor nurses for other patients, we got him setup to make his recycling purchases before he left. I never saw him after he was discharged. I'd like to think in my own small way, I made random butt stuff safer, during my general surgery rotation. At that moment, it was the tiny victories that counted.
